summary: Provides guidance to authors and reviewers of new protocols and extensions on considering operations and management from the start. Retrofitting manageability later is harder, so it offers a checklist of questions to address. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5706 asks protocol designers to consider how people will install, run, monitor, and manage a protocol while it is being designed. Its checklist helps authors and reviewers find operational questions that might otherwise be missed.

subtitle: Questions protocol designers should consider before deployment and management become difficult.

tldr.problem: Protocols are often designed without enough attention to deployment, operation, and management. Adding these capabilities later can be difficult and may conflict with earlier design choices.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5706 offers operational and management guidelines, advice on documenting decisions, and a review checklist. It distinguishes running a protocol from managing it with management protocols and data models.
tldr.outcome: The Informational document is advisory: it does not require a particular management protocol, formal data model, or solution. Designers should make decisions explicit rather than omit the topic.

sections.title: Consider Operations from the Start
sections.content:
Retrofitting operations and management features can be difficult, and some protocol design choices make deployment or troubleshooting harder. RFC 5706 encourages designers and working groups to consider these needs early, explain how they might be met, and identify useful management protocols or data models.

The document distinguishes operational considerations, which concern running a protocol in a network, from management considerations, which concern management technologies. It does not prescribe a solution: a working group may decide that a command-line interface is sufficient, but the decision should be explicit.
sections.plainLanguage: Think about how a protocol will be installed and operated while its design can still account for those needs. If no special management support is needed, record that decision and why.

sections.title: Fit the Protocol into a Network
sections.content:
Designers should consider how the protocol works with sensible defaults, how it will be installed, and whether operators can retrieve its actual settings. They should plan for coexistence with older versions, incremental deployment, and dependencies on other protocols or network components.

The RFC also asks designers to consider effects on network scale, traffic patterns, infrastructure such as DNS, and other protocols. They should provide ways to test end-to-end and per-device operation, including simple status or health indicators.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators need to know how to configure, upgrade, and test a protocol. Designers should also consider how it affects other network services and traffic.

sections.title: Make Management Information Useful
sections.content:
Management planning begins by identifying what entities need to be managed and how the protocol will be installed, configured, and monitored. The document cautions that managing one device endpoint is not always enough to manage a protocol between endpoints or the service built from it.

Information models can help different tools give information the same meaning, even when they use different management protocols. The RFC recommends separating configuration, operational state, and statistics; starting with essential information; and considering fault, configuration, accounting, performance, and security management.
sections.plainLanguage: Decide what information operators need and keep settings, current state, and statistics distinct. A counter should mean the same thing when different tools report it.

sections.title: Document the Decisions and Review Them
sections.content:
The RFC recommends a Manageability Considerations section that discusses relevant topics and briefly explains when a topic does not apply. If an extension relies on the base protocol's guidance, the document should point readers to it. The section is recommended immediately before Security Considerations.

Appendix A provides a review checklist covering operational impact, setup, migration, interoperability, faults, configuration, accounting, performance, security management, and documentation. RFC 5706 deliberately does not use RFC 2119 keywords: its guidance is not an interoperability requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: Write down the management and operations questions the design considered, including why some do not apply. The appendix offers a checklist that authors and reviewers can use.
